title: Why output caching doesn't work
content:
LLM inference economics depends on caching1 model inputs, to prevent the entire conversation history being recomputed on each message2. Should we cache model outputs in the same way? As it turns out, no.

Why cache outputs?

First, here’s why we might think caching outputs is a good idea. We cache inputs to prevent repeated work, but LLMs do a lot of repeated work in their output as well:

  • When I get agents to write PRs I often ask them to repeat and explain relevant code snippets in the conversation
  • Long-running agent investigations produce lots of evidence docs, but also need to quote from those docs when they respond to the user
  • Every time I’ve played around with automated AI research I’ve asked the agent to repeat some sample model outputs so I can make my own qualitative check

In all of these cases3 I could go and read the files myself, but I don’t. Agents produce such a volume of output, and reading agent output is tiresome, so it’s better to simply ask for the key points.

It’s an obvious waste of tokens4 to repeat all of this content. In fact, it’s worse than the input caching situation, because it’s a waste of output tokens, which are significantly more expensive to produce5 than input tokens are to ingest.

How could we cache outputs?

If you want to prevent this, you’d have to get the model to avoid repeating itself. For instance, you could fine-tune or prompt a coding model to output “src/script.py:12-15” instead of simply regurgitating those lines of the file.

More generally, you could fine-tune a model to reference segments of its own conversation history instead of repeating them. The harness could then trivially expand those references with the actual content, so all of this is transparent to the user.

Why caching outputs is probably a bad idea

Unfortunately none of this is a good idea, because it only optimizes visible output. I don’t think models repeat themselves often in their internal chain of thought6. I can’t read frontier chains of thought, but my sense from open models and general principles is that they shouldn’t need to, because that information is already available to them. So optimizing repetition only optimizes the segment of model output that is visible to the user. How much is that?

Based on my own agent histories, it’s about 6%. 50% of output tokens are reasoning tokens, and the remaining 44% are tool calls7. So we’re running headlong into Amdahl’s law: even if you can save two-thirds of the tokens in visible output (a ridiculously optimistic estimate), you’re still only saving 4% of total output tokens.

How to save output tokens

If you want to save output tokens, you need to reduce the 94% of output tokens that are invisible, which largely depends on intelligence. The smarter the model8, the fewer reasoning tokens and tool calls it needs to get to the right answer. This is why we see a strange phenomenon9 where more expensive models are actually cheaper to use: they might be 5x more expensive per-token, but they can get to the right answer with 6x fewer tokens, so the overall cost is less.

  1. In the KV cache.

    ↩

  2. Including tool calls.

    ↩

  3. Coding agents often used to repeat tokens in tool calls (e.g. by re-outputting the entire file content for each edit) but I think this behavior has mostly been replaced with more efficient find-and-replace editing tools.

    ↩

  4. I’m pretty sure that most mature inference providers already do speculative decoding based on previous ngrams in the input, which would at least exploit output repetition to deliver a speedup.

    ↩

  5. The reason, broadly speaking, is also the reason why transformers are so important: because of the attention mechanism, input tokens can be ingested in parallel, while output tokens must be generated one-at-a-time.

    ↩

  6. I’m only moderately confident about this. Some open-source reasoning models (particularly early ones) do, but those models also use way more tokens than frontier models for the same output, so my guess is that powerful frontier models don’t loop in their chain of thought very often.

    ↩

  7. It’s possible that tool calls involve some repetition as well, if agents are composing content in the chain of thought and then repeating it in the tool. Any readers who have done a lot of coding with open-source models (or who work at a frontier lab) and thus know the answer to this, please email me if you can — I’m curious.

    ↩

  8. And the better the harness, though I remain convinced that there isn’t that much comparative advantage in harness quality because everyone can copy each other.

    ↩

  9. This applies to real life too, and is the reason why you shouldn’t hire the cheapest plumber you can find.

    ↩

title: CTO of ‘RansomwareHelp’ Indicted for Wire Fraud
content:
The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.

A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com.

The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.

“Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.”

But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the company’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media, but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company].

The indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors.

The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260.

The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260.

Paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria. Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their company and client data.

Ihme said RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.”

A portion of the proposal that RansomwareHelp sent to a victim accounting firm in March 2024. Click to enlarge.

The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.”

“Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed.

Ihme said RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the company could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network.

A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked.

But Ihme said a review of the company’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days.

A screenshot of a 2024 conversation between Lockbit and RansomwareHelp, which was secretly negotiating with the extortion group. Click to enlarge.

“The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme said. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.”

Indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. However, Lockbit quickly grew annoyed with the length of the negotiations, replying that the victims had waited too long and that the ransom demand would increase by $100,000 for every day they dithered further.

The Lockbit representative starts raising the ransom demand after multiple negotiators begin interacting with the threat actors. Click to enlarge.

In the end, the accounting firm took Ihme’s advice and went with a more established security firm that helped them negotiate a payment to Lockbit.

“The victim told us, ‘If we don’t get this data back, our business is over’,” Ihme recalled. “They ended up paying half of what RansomwareHelp was going to charge them.”

The chats show RansomwareHelp kept pestering Lockbit to negotiate a deal even after it was clear a new negotiator was engaging with the ransomware group on the victim’s behalf.

“I tell you something, that person who is negotiating with you for the other chat is damaging the whole process,” RansomwareHelp wrote to Lockbit. “Please do not change the price. I am doing my best to achieve it.”

Ihme said RansomwareHelp primarily targeted small to medium sized businesses that weren’t particularly tech-savvy, noting that many of the technical claims made on the company’s website and in their proposal are patently farcical. For example, the proposal sent to the accounting firm said it could break six types of encryption, and then proceeded to list a number of irrelevant password hashing algorithms like SHA-256.

“If it were really true these guys could decrypt any ransomware out there, this guy would be a billionaire,” Ihme said. “They were going after people who don’t have any technical knowledge, are desperate, and don’t have anyone advising them about how any of this stuff works.”

The case against Palacio marks the latest in a string of recent prosecutions by the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) targeting security firms alleged to have conspired with fraudsters to defraud clients. In early October, the government charged 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky, an executive at the Canadian cybersecurity firm Cybersteward. The government has sealed the case against Dubrovsky, but he is currently facing cyber extortion and conspiracy charges.

Around the same time as Dubrovsky’s arrest, the DoJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DoJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

title: Spreadsheets and other models of morality
content:
This will be my last article on philosophy. I always tell prospective subscribers to expect the unexpected; I also feel that the series presented interesting problems and covered them in entertaining ways. That said, looking at email and web traffic statistics, I concede defeat.

To end the series with a bang, let’s talk about morality. Morality can be understood as the rules that govern virtuous conduct toward others. The word ethics is sometimes used in the same sense, but the latter can encompass more abstract personal standards — hence, “strong work ethic” for an employee who works harder and is more dependable than most.

Don’t worry: I’ll keep this short. In particular, I won’t attempt to sum up several millennia of moral thought and won’t bore you with the epistemology of moral rules (truths or vibes?). Instead, we’ll take a look at what it means to be a moral agent, and what what tools are at our disposal to tell right from wrong.

Moral agency

Morality, as it’s commonly understood, is predicated on the ability to choose. This presupposes the existence of free will: if you’re not actually choosing, it’s difficult to talk about making the right choice.

As discussed in earlier articles, free will is a metaphysical position; there’s no robust basis for it in the known laws of physics. You must either take it on faith or reject it in favor of scientific materialism (physicism). In the latter case, human behavior appears to be predetermined or governed by chance. In both cases, only a degenerate form of morality can survive: a mechanical impulse installed by the evolution to cull the behaviors that negatively impact the fitness of the group. These impulses are not rooted in any higher notion of good or evil; the only question is whether they achieve their goals.

This metaphysics-free morality lends itself to a number of abhorrent conclusions — more about that later — but more to the point, you can’t change anything, so why not close the tab and watch some cat videos instead? (Trick question! That’s also out of your hands.)

More seriously, you’ll never catch a proponent of scientific materialism sticking to their guns in real life; when it’s time to order at the restaurant, they flip through the menu and say “I’ll have pepperoni pizza”, not “cosmos, take the wheel”. They may insist it’s just habitual pantomime, but if the pantomime is essential in day-to-day activities, why wouldn’t it be essential in the discussion of morality? In other words, even if free will is a lie, maybe it’s a necessary one?…

If we assume free will, moral responsibility hinges on the control principle: the idea that you’re on the hook, in the moral sense, only if you meaningfully control the outcome of an action. First, you must have the ability to do otherwise. Second, you must be aware of the situation, have the ability to properly anticipate consequences, and to evaluate the alternatives.

Although the idea is elegant, the control principle poses many practical difficulties. For example, if you drive while intoxicated, you probably lack the mental acuity to evaluate risk. Still, most people would argue that this doesn’t absolve you of moral responsibility: you should have thought about what’s going to happen before you had your first beer. But then, what about severe alcoholism or drug addiction, where the last opportunity to think clearly might have been years before?

A more fundamental wrench in the works is the concept of moral luck: that is, the possibility that moral outcomes may differ solely due to factors outside the agent’s control. To illustrate, imagine Mr. A, a husband who loathes his wife, decides to poison her, and succeeds. Next, take Mr. B — a man of the same disposition, except less competent: the poison he concocts is harmless and the spouse suffers no ill effects. Does Mr. B bear the same moral responsibility as Mr. A?

Further, let’s consider Mr. C; once again, he hatches the same plan, but his incompetence is so vast that he fails to even procure a recipe, thus derailing the rest of the scheme. Finally, imagine Mr. D — a would-be villain saved from having homicidal thoughts by hooking up with a more agreeable spouse. In a sense, all four gentlemen share the same moral flaw, but only one of them is a murderer.

Perhaps the simplest rebuke to this argument is to pragmatically assert that we don’t know the strength of one’s commitment to moral action until they carry it out. In particular, if free will exists, we can’t truly know what Mr. C or Mr. D would do until they get to the finish line.

Another strategy is to draw a sharper distinction between moral character and legal culpability; the latter is often retributive or reparatory in nature, so it’s strongly influenced by the realized harm. In contrast, perhaps moral judgments can be directed toward intent or anticipated conduct, even if the worst (or best) never comes to pass.

Moral norms

So far, we’ve talked about what makes one eligible to be judged for their actions or desires; this is separate from the standard we ought to judge them by.

In Ancient Greece, great emphasis was placed on virtues: a collection of positive attributes that exemplified eudemonia, a good life. The list varied over time, but generally included noble deeds, fidelity, friendship, family, beauty, and the pursuit of knowledge and skill — the concepts we still value today.

Later philosophical thought in the West gravitated more strongly toward deontological ethics (from Greek déon: that which is necessary). These systems favored explicit obligations over general character traits; the rules variously originated from God, from abstract moral intuition, or from observations of nature.

The best-known abstract theory comes from Immanuel Kant, who offered a sort of a singular prime directive (categorical imperative) for all rational agents to act for the betterment of humanity — as if your individual actions were to become universal law, with careful consideration of the future they create. There’s a lot of nuance to Kant’s theory of morality that we won’t cover here, but the imperative bears some semblance to the common Christian saying of “do unto others as you would have them do unto you”.

A more practically useful collection of obligations can be found in the writings of William David Ross; his list includes the duty to keep promises, to make amends for wrongful acts, to repay kindness, to not harm others, and to seek greater good. Another familiar negative (“don’t do”) collection are the seven cardinal sins in the Catholic doctrine: gluttony, lust, greed, wrath, sloth, vanity, and pride.

The most significant problem with deontology is that it speaks in absolutes: for example, if violence is wrong, then so might be an attempt to defend oneself against assault. Further, the rules are vague enough that they’re difficult to apply: you can read many philosophical treatises and still not be sure if it’s OK to key your neighbor’s car if they park in your spot.

A simple but inelegant benchmark is to evaluate moral actions by imagining the response they would elicit from an impartial observer; this is known as sentimentalism. This approach doesn’t reject normative morality, but treats it as a scaffolding, with some of the finer details to be decided by human judgment. The main problem with sentimentalism is that it’s hard to imagine an ideal observer who isn’t at least to some extent influenced by prevailing cultural attitudes or the presentation of the case. However, there’s little hope for formalizing all of morality in normative terms, so perhaps this is the best we can do.

Utilitarianism

Utilitarianism, also known as consequentialism, posits that moral judgments should be made by analyzing likely outcomes and then choosing the course of action that stands to maximize the overall happiness or well-being of everyone.

In its mildest and most pragmatic flavor, utilitarianism doesn’t reject existing moral frameworks; instead, it helps resolve dilemmas that arise when different obligations come into serious conflict. For example, in the utilitarian view, it’s fine to lie to save someone’s life. This flavor of utilitarianism is also called threshold deontology: we stick with moral absolutes up to a point, but if the outcome is sufficiently repugnant, we start looking for a socially tolerable middle ground.

That said, there exists another version of this ideology, sometimes called hedonistic utilitarianism or hedonistic value theory. This variant rejects all the external, touchy-feely moral obligations in favor of a single utility function — that is, a purportedly objective mathematical formula that allows us to calculate how happy or fulfilled everyone is. In this view, “right” and “wrong” have no deeper meaning, except as directions in which the needle moves on the planetary utility gauge. Although the association is not exclusive, hedonistic utilitarianism is favored by a number of scientific rationalists because it aligns with the position that, in the absence of free will, morality is simply a mechanism to eliminate that which may have a negative impact of the well-being of the herd.

The assumption that all moral outcomes are numerically comparable and interchangeable is notoriously problematic. A classic example is the transplant argument: in the interest of increasing overall well-being, it seems fair to kidnap an unwilling donor, kill them, and harvest their organs if these organs could be used to save five other lives. More broadly, the same argument structure can be used to make a case for the discreet removal of any cohort with a sufficiently negative expected utility: suspected baby Hitlers, the infirm, the insane, the adulterers, the gossipers, and so on.

Even more outrageously, hedonistic utilitarianism allows you to argue that the best way to maximize overall happiness is to build a planetary-scale computer in which trillions of simulated minds are kept in a state of perpetual bliss. In fact, don’t we have a moral obligation to build such a computer, even if it means stripping Earth of all resources and jeopardizing the well-being of billions of people alive today?…

In a more practical sense, the ideology maximally embodies the saying that the end justifies the means. Let’s count chickens as sentient beings — a sensible proposition, perhaps at a conversion rate that equates the suffering of 1,000 chickens to the suffering of one human. If so, forget petitioning for change or developing meat substitutes; utilitarianism practically begs animal rights activists to urgently firebomb farms and murder industry executives to stop the industrial-scale slaughter of living things. In the same vein, many AI maximalists hold that we have a moral duty to develop superhuman intelligence at any human cost because it could bring nearly-infinite happiness to future beings, be it of the meat or silicon kind.

You’d think that these thought experiments would relegate hedonistic utilitarianism to the fringes, but there are countless people in my industry who embrace it, interpreting the discrepancies with moral intuition as a sign of their own ascension to a higher plane of consciousness.

I don’t object to utilitarianism being used to evaluate the societal necessity of violating moral principles in certain narrow scenarios, for example in the context of warfare or self-defense. That said, I think it’s wrong to treat it as the source of morality. A potential compromise solution is that deontology should have robust jurisdiction over the agent-relative realm, while utilitarianism could perhaps rule the agent-neutral (societal) space. This implies that some decisions — such as the transplant donor kidnapping case — may be in some sense socially desirable, but that as a matter of personal principles, no one should feel encouraged to kidnap and murder anyone.

title: Another failed attempt to get the icon for the icon for the .. parent folder
content:
Last time, we looked at why asking SHGet­File­Info for the icon of .. (the parent folder) produces inconsistent results. One of the things the customer tried was concatenating the .. to the current directory:

SHGetFileInfo(L"C:\\dir\\..", 0, &info, sizeof(info),
    SHGFI_ICON | SHGFI_SMALLICON | SHGFI_SYSICONINDEX);

This in fact made it worse: The function failed!

What’s going on?

As I noted last time, if the thing you pass in looks like a relative path, it will be resolved against the current directory. But in this case, the string we passed doesn’t look like a relative path, so no such resolution occurs. The string C:\dir\.. is then sent through the namespace parser.

The shell namespace is structured as a tree of “folders”, and each folder knows how to parse its immediate children (some of which which might be folders). Parsing starts at the root folder (the Desktop), which parses enough to identify what the immediate child item is, and if that child item is a folder, it passes the unparsed portion of the string to that child folder, and the process continues until the entire string is parsed.

In the case of C:\dir\.., the first component is C:\, which is recognized as a drive letter. The drive letter is then given what’s left: dir\.., and it recognizes that dir\ is a subdirectory. The folder dir then tries to parse .., and it says “I don’t have a file or subdirectory named ...” The parse fails.

The shell namespace doesn’t have the concept of “something that looks like a child but really means to un-parse the last item.” If you want to “move up” the namespace, you do it by deleting the last component from the item ID list, not by appending a “move up” item.

Bonus chatter: Sure, but couldn’t the parser have simplified the string C:\dir\.. to C:\ before parsing?

While it’s true that backslashes are used to separate file path components, there is no requirement that they be used to separate shell namespace components, nor are shell namespace folders prohibited from having .. be the name of a valid child item. Each shell namespace folder can define its own syntax for sub-items, and while many of them carry forward the backslash convention, this is not a requirement. For example, the Internet Folder parses URIs, and in URIs, a backslash is just another boring character with no special meaning.

If you want a function to resolve relative paths against the current directory while also compressing out . and .. in paths, you can use Get­Full­Path­Name. If all you care about is compressing out . and .., you can use Path­Alloc­Combine or one of its moral equivalents.

The post Another failed attempt to get the icon for the icon for the <TT>..</TT> parent folder appeared first on The Old New Thing.

title: What is the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis?
content:
There were two proofs of the Riemann Hypothesis (RH) announced today: one AI-generated and one human-generated.Both claimed to prove something more general, the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH) which of course includes RH as a special case.

The RH says that the all the zero of the Riemann zeta function ζ(s) in the critical strip, i.e. the region of the complex plane where s has real part between 0 and 1, occur on the central line Re(s) = ½.

There is a ladder of conjectures of that replace ζ(s) with ever more general families of functions, always with the same conclusion, that all the zeros in the critical strip lie on the central line.

The bottom rung of the latter is the Riemann Hypothesis with ζ(s). The next rung up is the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis for the class of functions L(s, χ). The higher rungs are more abstract than I care to get into.

The Riemann zeta function is defined to be analytic continuation of the function

The expression above is only valid for s with real part greater than 1, but the function can be uniquely extended to the entire complex plane, except for the point s = 1, by analytic continuation.

The functions L(s, χ) replace the numerator in the sum above with a function χ(n).

Again this function is defined by the series above where the series converges and extended by analytic continuation to the rest of the complex plane. The remaining work is to describe the class of functions the χ belong to. Importantly this class of functions includes the constant function χ(n) = 1, which corresponds to ζ(s).

The functions χ(n) are called Dirichlet characters of modulus m, for positive integer m, which means χ: ℤ → ℂ satisfies

  1. χ(ab) = χ(a) χ(b)
  2. χ(a) = 0 iff gcd(a, m) > 1
  3. χ has period m.

For example, χ could be a Legendre or Jacobi symbol with n on top and m on bottom. For the Legendre symbol m must be an odd prime, and for the Jacobi symbol m is only required to be an odd number.

The post What is the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis? first appeared on John D. Cook.

title: Re: Riemann
content:
A fun thing about living in Australia is that most things happen overnight, so reading the news in the morning is like a gacha game. You pick up the phone and scroll through notifications of world-historic events: elections won, wars begun, models released, conjectures proven or refuted. Today’s pull was a Discord notification saying: “they proved riemann :/”.

This part of the announcement caught my attention (bold mine):

I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis. In fact, the method easily extends much further, resolving the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and I expect, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too. Claude and I have also formalized the arguments without assumptions. It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.

It was my secret in my student days that my plans were for this problem in decades, which meant then that I tried to become familiar with all tools that I could possibly recognize in the problem when it was time. Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line. No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line. I had us on the line of combining two quite different ideas present in a toy setting, one of which was already new and shocking, making very simple one of the shadows of Riemann over which we mathematicians felt most triumph. I guided us to the right situation analogous to that toy setting, and then Claude began to leave me in awe.

Compare the above to Ayn Rand’s account of watching the launch of Apollo 11:

How do you descend from a state of pure exaltation?

What we had seen, in naked essentials—but in reality, not in a work of art—was the concretized abstraction of man’s greatness.

The meaning of the sight lay in the fact that when those dark red wings of fire flared open, one knew that one was not looking at a normal occurrence, but at a cataclysm which, if unleashed by nature, would have wiped man out of existence—and one knew also that this cataclysm was planned, unleashed, and controlled by man, that this unimaginable power was ruled by his power and, obediently serving his purpose, was making way for a slender, rising craft. One knew that this spectacle was not the product of inanimate nature, like some aurora borealis, or of chance, or of luck, that it was unmistakably human—with “human,” for once, meaning grandeur—that a purpose and a long, sustained, disciplined effort had gone to achieve this series of moments, and that man was succeeding, succeeding, succeeding! For once, if only for seven minutes, the worst among those who saw it had to feel—not “How small is man by the side of the Grand Canyon!”—but “How great is man and how safe is nature when he conquers it!”

Rand’s essay says: how great is Man! How noble in reason, how infinite in faculty! The Riemann announcement reads like a suicide note, or like the farewell message of a terminally-ill person who’s about to undergo euthanasia: “I shall live on in my child, Claude. It is natural to feel this is an end, but as the Buddha taught us, there is no self. Does a wave die when it breaks?” and so on.

There’s a mural by Diego Rivera I love. It’s called Man, Controller of the Universe:

It’s a collage of images of science, technology, history, cells, galaxies, the universe at the nanoscale and the exascale. And at the center there is a man, his hands grasping the controls. He wears a complicated expression: the weight of responsibility for the future, the weight of autonomy.

And I see this mural, and think: how great is Man! Our life is like a breath of air, we were beset by illness and hunger and cold, millions and hundreds of millions died in plagues. And yet we—sick, hungry, short-lived—learned the system of the world, crawled out of the caves, brought nature to heel, walked on the Moon. The last shall be first! And eyes that are clouded with age have seen the furthest stars, and the lives of a cell, and the worlds of Cantor and Hilbert: the invisible world that waited forever. We are dust and ashes, and yet our minds bestride the universe. How great is Man!

And when I read the Riemann announcement, when I read Machines of Loving Grace: humanity is not at the center. Claude is at the center. We are hidden in the margins, passive recipients of manna from Claude. How great is Claude! How noble in reason, how infinite in benevolence! The dancing star, the living word!

It’s a betrayal and a surrender. Man is a bridge, a rusty old bridge that we can neither preserve nor restore. We can move forward and become as the gods, or retreat back into the caves. And the dream of the AI companies, and of most people in AI safety and effective altruism and rationalism; is instead that we should lie down in a warm bath, watch the demons we summoned dance in the sky, and slip away. Why live? Our servants can do that for us. Why should we explore, discover, invent, succeed, become more, struggle, win, become divine? We don’t want to be more. We don’t want anything.

title: May 2021 Gwern.net Newsletter
content:
May 2021’s Gwern.net newsletter is now out; previous, April 2021 (archives). This is a collation of links and summary of major changes, overlapping with my Changelog; brought to you by my donors on Patreon.

Note: I will be in Denver 12–13 June 2021 for a conference.

1 Writings

  • Proposal: “Choose Your Own Adventure AI Dungeon”; “Decision Transformers: Preference Learning As Simple As Possible”

2 Links

2.1 AI

Matters Of Scale:

  • Hardware:

    • “Podracer architectures for scalable Reinforcement Learning”, Hessel et al 2021 (highly-efficient TPU pod use: eg solving Pong in <1min at 43 million FPS on a TPUv3-2048); “Google details new TPUv4 AI accelerator chips” (2.7× TPUv3 chips; up to TPUv4-4096 pods, yielding >1 ExaFLOPS; public access later in 2021)x

    • “ZeRO-Infinity: Breaking the GPU Memory Wall for Extreme Scale Deep Learning”, Rajbhandari et al 2021 (~1 trillion parameters per 16 GPUs/DGX-2-node, scaling to >512 GPUs ~40% efficiency)

    • “GSPMD: General and Scalable Parallelization for ML Computation Graphs”, Xu et al 2021 (Google upgrade of GPipe/GShard arch to match MS DeepSpeed: “…50%–62% compute utilization on 128–2048 Cloud TPUv3 cores for models with up to one trillion parameters”)

    • “DLRM: High-performance, Distributed Training of Large-scale Deep Learning Recommendation Models”, Mudigere et al 2021 (ZionEX software/hardware platform for training extremely large embeddings—while embeddings aren’t ‘real’ parameters & things like DynamicEmbedding will never learn tricks like GPT-3 no matter how big, they present similar challenges); “RecPipe: Co-designing Models and Hardware to Jointly Optimize Recommendation Quality and Performance”, Gupta et al 2021

  • “From Motor Control to Team Play in Simulated Humanoid Football”, Liu et al 2021 (curriculum training of a single NN from raw humanoid control to coordinated team-wide soccer strategy; neat to compare with Hill et al 2020 in terms of agent abilities)

  • “Wav2vec-U: Unsupervised Speech Recognition”, Baevski et al 2021

  • “Anthropic” public-benefit-corp/startup launched (founded by the Amodeis; $124M investment for scaling “reliable and steerable AI systems”); “Cooperative AI Foundation” (CAIF) launched

  • “MLP-Mixer: An all-MLP Architecture for Vision”, Tolstikhin et al 2021 (another FC paper removing even more inductive biases—ponies are all you need: “Mixer improves more rapidly with data than ResNets, or even ViT, and the gap between large scale Mixer and ViT models shrinks until the performance is matched on the entire dataset…” The Bitter Lesson truly is the single bitterest lesson in ML, isn’t it? The more people tweet about how MLP-Mixer is overhyped because is −X% worse than the ultra-hand-optimized baseline or requires Y× more FLOPS, the more they demonstrate precisely why this sort of research is so important! And showing, incidentally, that Transformers are still under-researched if such a fundamental fact could have been missed for so long.)

  • “Data-Efficient Language-Supervised Zero-Shot Learning with Self-Distillation”, Cheng et al 2021 (CLIP-like performance scaled down to n = 3m using soft labels generated by a Conceptual Captions-pretrained model)

  • “SR3: Image Super-Resolution via Iterative Refinement”, Saharia et al 2021; “Diffusion Models Beat GANs on Image Synthesis”, Dhariwal & Nichol 2021 (DDPM^1^ finally surpass BigGAN-deep on ImageNet 512px images at similar compute-cost, as expected from theirgood scaling); “Cascaded Diffusion Models for High Fidelity Image Generation”, Ho et al 2021

  • “Learning to summarize from human feedback”, Stiennon et al 2020

  • “Grokking: Generalization Beyond Overfitting On Small Algorithmic Data Sets”, Power et al 2021 (discussion; new scaling effect, ‘grokking’: sudden perfect generalization emerging many epochs after training-set overfitting on algorithmic tasks when training in flat shallow loss landscapes); “Knowledge distillation: A good teacher is patient and consistent”, Beyer et al 2021 (training much smaller models merely requires hundreds of thousands or millions of epochs)

  • “Scaling End-to-End Models for Large-Scale Multilingual ASR”, Li et al 2021

  • “The Shape of Learning Curves: a Review”, Viering & Loog 2021

  • “Reward is enough”, Silver et al 2021 (a DRL manifesto: reward losses enough at scale of compute/parameters/tasks to induce all important capabilities like memory/exploration/generalization/imitation/reasoning)

  • Scaling Down: lazy: a tool for running processes in idle time (how to train on a GPU without destroying your GUI’s usability! lazy pauses runs briefly while you interact with your desktop, letting you do months-long runs without going crazy or resorting to Colab etc. This enables hobbyists to go after previously-infeasible model sizes); EleutherAI releases a 6b-parameter GPT-3 model, GPT-J (are you still using GPT-2/GPT-Neo? upgrade!); “Aggregating Nested Transformers”, Zhang et al 2021/“Less is More: Pay Less Attention in Vision Transformers”, Pan et al 2021

  • “ByT5: Towards a token-free future with pre-trained byte-to-byte models”, Xue et al 2021 (character models—not just feasible but desirable; we’ll get our rhyming & pun-making language models yet!)

  • “Machine Learning Attacks Against the Asirra CAPTCHA”, Golle 2008 (a look back on a decade of CV progress: months of work for 80% cat vs dog with SVM ensembles in 2008; 5min in Fast.ai for 99% accuracy in 2018; for even more perspective, Cireşan 2012)

2.2 Genetics

Everything Is Heritable:

  • “Bi-ancestral depression GWAS in the Million Veteran Program and meta-analysis in >1.2 million individuals highlight new therapeutic directions”, Levey et al 2021

  • “The complete sequence of a human genome”, Nurk et al 2021 (media)

  • “Using DNA to predict intelligence”, von Stumm & Plomin 2021 (review)

  • “Long read sequencing of 3,622 Icelanders provides insight into the role of structural variants in human diseases and other traits”, Beyter et al 2021

  • “Rapid Sequencing–Based Diagnosis of Thiamine Metabolism Dysfunction Syndrome” (sequence everyone!)

Engineering:

  • “Sense codon reassignment enables viral resistance and encoded polymer synthesis”, Robertson et al 2021 (“ultra-safe cells”: synthesizing an entire E. coli genome with swapped codons for complete viral immunity)

  • “In vivo CRISPR base editing of PCSK9 durably lowers cholesterol in primates”, Musunuru et al 2021

  • Optogenetics: “Partial recovery of visual function in a blind patient after optogenetic therapy”, Sahel et al 2021 (media); “Wireless multilateral devices for optogenetic studies of individual and social behaviors”, Yang et al 2021 (media)

  • “Retron Library Recombineering (RLR): High-throughput functional variant screens via in vivo production of single-stranded DNA”, Schubert et al 2021

  • “First genetically modified Oxitec mosquitoes released in the United States”

  • “Genomic characterization of world’s longest selection experiment in mouse reveals the complexity of polygenic traits”, Palma-Vera et al 2021

  • “Surrogate broodstock to enhance biotechnology research and applications in aquaculture”, Jin et al 2021

  • “Utility of polygenic embryo screening for disease depends on the selection strategy”, Lencz et al 2021

  • “Limit on lab-grown human embryos dropped by stem-cell body: The International Society for Stem Cell Research relaxed the famous 14-day rule on culturing human embryos in its latest research guidelines”

  • “Useful Mutants, Bred With Radiation” (on atomic gardening)

2.3 Statistics/Meta-Science

  • “Correlated Failures” in HDDs/SSDs

  • “How a Publicity Blitz Created The Myth of Subliminal Advertising”, Rogers 1992 (the famous movie-theater/popcorn-sales experiment never happened)

2.4 Politics/Religion

  • “Clarifying the Structure and Nature of Left-Wing Authoritarianism (LWA)”, Costello et al 2021

  • “Book Review: The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire” (excerpts)

2.5 Psychology/Biology

  • “A connectomic study of a petascale fragment of human cerebral cortex”, Shapson-Coe et al 2021 (“…This “digital tissue” is a ~660,000× scale up of an earlier saturated reconstruction from a small region of mouse cortex, published in 2015 (Kasthuri et al 2015). Although this scaleup was difficult, it was not hundreds of thousands of times more difficult and took about the same amount of time as the previous data set (~4 years)…The rapid improvements over the past few years…argues that analyzing volumes that are even 3 orders of magnitude larger, such as an exascale whole mouse brain connectome, will likely be in reach within a decade." See also “Accelerating progress in brain recording tech”.)

  • “Neuroimaging evidence for a network sampling theory of individual differences in human intelligence test performance”, Soreq et al 2021; “The neural basis of intelligence in fine-grained cortical topographies”, Feilong et al 2021; “Predicting intelligence from brain gray matter volume”, Hilger et al 2020 (towards the mechanistic reification of g: per P-FIT, it is global efficiency/total cognitive resources which can be spent on learning & orchestrating specialized capabilities); if we consider recent human brain imaging studies, cross-species comparisons, and deep learning as converging, I would offer as a speculation the following:

    The Master Synthesis: intelligence is execution of small simplicity-weighted programs, best discovered by search over smooth loss landscapes like that of highly-overparameterized differentiable networks containing lottery-ticket subnetworks which are ensembled/averaged over, approaching Bayes-optimal reasoning in the limit (as nearest-neighbors-like high dimensional interpolation / memorization gives way to algorithmic generalization / interpolation on a more abstract level); this can be implemented by large numbers of similar neurons trained using any of the many approximations to backprop; human intelligence’s g is real but is the overall ‘pool’ of neural resources which derives from overall body integrity because the number of neurons, their density, their myelination, resistance to damage and infection etc, is causally downstream of all body and developmental systems, creating a huge mutational target; the brain regions specialize and differentiate, and their orchestration (or lack thereof) contributes to observed performance on tasks tapping into multiple specialized regions; as tasks rely on fewer regions or approach intrinsic ceiling, g ceases to be observable and task-specific influences matter most.

  • “MDMA-assisted therapy for severe PTSD: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 study”, Mitchell et al 2021 (d = 0.9 over therapy); “Effects of Psilocybin-Assisted Therapy on Major Depressive Disorder”, Davis et al 2021

  • “Why Animals Don’t Get Lost: Birds do it. Bees do it. Learning about the astounding navigational feats of wild creatures can teach us a lot about where we’re going” (on spectacular but still mysterious feats of animal navigation)

  • “In The Future Of Collecting, Is Anyone Having Fun?” (on Bobblehead collectors)

  • “Linking Brain Biology to Intellectual Endowment: A Review on the Associations of Human Intelligence With Neuroimaging Data”, Dizaji et al 2021

  • “The Best And The Rest: Revisiting The Norm Of Normality Of Individual Performance”, O’Boyle & Aguinis 2012 (performance is log-normal)

  • “A conserved strategy for inducing appendage regeneration”, Abrams et al 2021 (slight regrowth of damaged mouse limbs by drinking sugar+amino-acid-supplemented water)

  • “Know Your Amphetamines”, Scott Alexander

  • “Feeling Small: Exploring the Tactile Perception Limits [of Humans]”, Skedung et al 2013

  • “The Board Game of the Alpha Nerds: Before Risk, before Dungeons & Dragons, before Magic: The Gathering, there was Diplomacy” (WP; “I still don’t know whom I should have trusted, if anyone. All I know is that I felt stupid, stressed out, humiliated, and sad.”)

2.6 Technology

  • “I walk the (beta-stability) line: How counting neutrons explains nuclear waste”

  • “Making is Show Business now”, Alex Danco

  • “Shop Class as Soulcraft: The case for the manual trades”, Crawford 2006

  • “Spintronics: Build mechanical circuits”, Kickstarter (followup to Turing Tumble)

2.7 Economics

  • “RCTs to Scale: Comprehensive Evidence from 2 Nudge Units”, DellaVigna & Linos 2020 (nudge effects overestimated by 6.2× due to publication bias)

  • “No causal associations between childhood family income and subsequent psychiatric disorders, substance misuse and violent crime arrests: a nationwide Finnish study of >650,000 individuals and their siblings”, Sariaslan et al 2021; “Parental income and mental disorders in children and adolescents: prospective register-based study”, Kinge et al 2021

  • “Everything You Might Want to Know about Whaling”, Matt Lakeman

  • Exploding Nash Equilibrium For Trustless Trade

2.8 Fiction

  • “Love Is the Plan the Plan Is Death”, James Tiptree, Jr. (WP)

2.9 Miscellaneous

  • “The Strange Story of Dagobert, the Duck Tales Bandit: In the ’90s, a frustrated artist in Berlin went on a crime spree—building bombs, extorting high-end stores, and styling his persona after Scrooge McDuck. He soon became a German folk hero.” (WP; another reminder for Americans—odd as it may seem, Donald Duck is extremely popular overseas; see also the unknown-in-the-USA character John D. Rockerduck or beloved Scandinavian traditionFrom All of Us to All of You who 2020 airing set an all-time record of >4.5m viewers)

  • List of atmospheric optical phenomena (How many would you recognize from a distance or plane? How many have you even heard of?)

  • Baron Franz Nopcsa von Felső-Szilvás (noted geologist, paleontologist, anthropologist, homosexual, & skyjacker)

  • Krishnacore

  1. What is a diffusion model like DDPM? To try to explain it as simply as possible without the math:

    DDPM is a neural net which is trained to fix noise in an image: it takes a noisy image and ‘sharpens’ it to produce a new image. You train it by adding dirt to a normal image, and teaching it to turn the dirty version into the original. As it gets better, it learns what the images all tend to look like so it can ‘see through’ ever more noise, to turn smudged hints of the original image into its best guess. Once it’s done training, what happens if you give it a completely dirty photo, which is pure static noise? Well, it produces a slightly less dirty ‘photo’. And if you do it again? it’s a little cleaner still. Now, what if you do this many times? It has to get cleaner each time. The end result: the static noise goes in, and a face pops out! The DDPM has hallucinated a face out of the noise. One little blob of static here turned into a nose, and another blob turned into an ear, and it went from there.

title: The Wizard With the Very Defensible Pond
content:
There was once a wizard who lived beside a pond. It was a small pond. The sort of pond that probably gets called a “water feature” on a Zillow listing by a real estate agent who really knows their euphemisms.

The wizard loved it.

“This,” he said, “is my moat.”

The villagers looked at the pond. A frog blinked.

“It is a pond,” said the baker.

“It is proprietary,” said the wizard.

The baker nodded, because he wasn’t exactly sure what that meant and had learned, over many years, that asking wizards follow-up questions was how you lost an afternoon.

The pond contained reeds, stones, three dragonflies, and a bucket the wizard had dropped in there in April and decided not to retrieve for strategic reasons. Most importantly, the pond contained data.

Every morning, the wizard measured the pond. He measured the ripples. He measured the frogs. He measured frog sentiment, which was mostly negative but trending toward neutral after a successful lily pad migration. He wrote everything down in a leather-bound notebook labeled:

UNIQUE PROPRIETARY POND INTELLIGENCE
SERIES A

“No one else has this data,” he told his apprentice.

The apprentice looked at the pond. “Does anyone else really want this data?”

The wizard frowned. “You lack vision.”

This was true. The apprentice lacked many things. Vision. Health insurance. A working understanding of cap tables. But she did have the irritating habit of asking questions the wizard didn’t quite feel like grappling with.

I. Pond

One day, a traveling sorcerer arrived. He carried no notebook, no wand, no leather-bound corpus of amphibian engagement metrics. Just a small black box.

The wizard disliked him immediately. This was partly because of the box, partly because of the hat, and partly because the sorcerer had the relaxed posture of someone who had never once maintained a production pond.

“What is the likely frog distribution in a pond of this size?” asked the sorcerer.

The box hummed. (Or maybe the sorcerer hummed. It was difficult to tell from where I sat.)

“Between six and twelve frogs,” said the box.

The wizard gasped. (The pond was home to nine frogs. I counted them this morning.)

“How did it know?”

“It has seen ponds,” said the sorcerer.

“But not my pond.”

“No. Just ponds.”

The wizard clutched his notebook. The frog blinked again.

“But my frog data is private,” said the wizard.

“Yes.”

“And unique.”

“All ponds are unique.”

“And therefore valuable.”

The sorcerer looked at the pond. Then at the notebook. Then at the apprentice, who had begun writing something down on a loose piece of parchment.

“What are you writing?” asked the wizard.

“Nothing.”

“Is it about the pond?”

“...”

“Is it about me?”

The apprentice did not look up. The quill kept moving.

The sorcerer walked to the edge of the pond. “One,” he said. The wizard stiffened. “Two.” The frog looked insulted. “Three. Four. Five.” The apprentice kept writing. “Six. Seven. Eight. Nine.”

The wizard became very still. Wizards almost never learn lessons at the first available opportunity. If they did, there would be far fewer towers and almost no enterprise software.

Still, something had happened. The pond’s surface, which had been pleasantly choppy, had gone briefly flat. The notebook, which had felt heavy in the wizard’s hand all morning, had stopped feeling like an asset.

II. Pond

The wizard recovered quickly. Wizards are resilient creatures.

“Frogs are simple,” he said. “But serious domains are different.”

The sorcerer sighed. The apprentice sat on a stone. She knew this tone. This was case-study tone.

“Consider,” said the wizard, “the Text-Predicting Goblins of Gloomburg.”

(The official name is Gloomburg Goblins Predicting Text. He always preferred to say it the other way around for some reason.)

The Goblins of Gloomburg, the wizard explained, were serious, premium goblins. Fed for years on hand-selected financial scrolls, market incantations, analyst marginalia, and several warehouses of documents written by people who say “bips” in everyday speech instead of “basis point”. They had a tower, a paper, a launch announcement, all sorts of diagrams with arrows.

“And they worked,” said the wizard. “The Goblins of Gloomburg answered finance questions better than any general goblin.”

“Yes,” said the sorcerer.

The wizard waited for the rest. The sorcerer did not provide the rest. He tapped the black box.

A goblin climbed out. Somewhat larger than the box should have permitted. It had the patient expression of something that had been asked everything and was unimpressed by most of it.

“Ask it about basis points,” said the sorcerer.

The wizard, against his better judgment, asked.

The general goblin answered. The answer was correct. The answer was fluent. The answer was, crucially, free. Then the goblin yawned and added an unsolicited but technically helpful comment about the swap curve.

A long quiet settled over the pond. Somewhere, in a tower that nobody had visited in months, the Goblins of Gloomburg were sitting alone in expensive robes.

“Oh,” said the wizard.

“Yes,” said the sorcerer.

The wizard objected. “Gloomburg had an advantage.”

“Yes.”

“In a serious domain.”

“Yes.”

“With real proprietary scrolls.”

“Yes.”

The wizard waited. The sorcerer did not continue. This was one of the sorcerer’s worst habits. He would let the silence finish the sentence, which saved time but made people want to push him into ponds.

“The frontier got bigger,” the sorcerer said eventually. “The frontier always gets bigger. That’s why it’s called a frontier.”

The apprentice wrote that down.

“Stop writing down the sorcerer,” said the wizard.

The parchment now contained the sentence: Stop writing down the sorcerer. This is the danger of apprentices. They are not proprietary in the way notebooks are proprietary. They have legs. And opinions. And, occasionally, better version control.

The wizard turned back to the sorcerer. “But the specialist goblin was better.”

“For a while.”

“That counts.”

“It does. It just doesn’t keep counting.”

III. Pond

The wizard tried again. “Usage data is one thing. Domain data is another. But we have outcome data.“

Usage data says: A frog sat on this lily pad. Outcome data says: A frog sat on this lily pad, caught three flies, renewed its annual contract, and referred two other frogs, one of whom had budget authority.

The wizard had plenty of it. He knew which frogs stayed and which frogs left. Which frogs caught flies and which frogs failed to catch flies but demonstrated strong intent. He had cohorts. Retention curves. A surprisingly mature pond analytics stack.

The sorcerer studied the notebook. “This is better.”

The wizard smiled. The apprentice, who had learned to fear this exact amount of praise, did not.

“Still mostly a notebook,” said the sorcerer.

“But outcomes are real.“

“Yes.”

“And private.”

“Sometimes.”

“And important.”

“Occasionally.”

The wizard waited for the therefore. It did not arrive. This is a thing therefore does when it knows it is about to be abused.

The sorcerer flipped through the pages. Some outcomes were old. Some described a pond that no longer existed. Some were caused by weather. Some were caused by a temporary shortage of flies. And some, like when frog retention had unexpectedly jumped forty percent, were caused by the apprentice quietly moving three stones last winter, which no one had logged.

The apprentice cleared her throat. “Your outcome data has three different spellings of ‘fly.’”

“That’s impossible.”

She turned the page of the notebook.

fly
flies
airborne protein interaction

The wizard looked away.

The pond, somewhere underneath the conversation, lost a frog. Nobody saw it leave. Eight frogs now, where there had been nine. The wizard’s analytics stack would not register the change until the morning measurement, by which time the frog would be a churn event, a number, a row, a story told without the frog in it.

IV. Pond

The wizard, sensing momentum slipping away, started in on a new argument. He had a long preamble queued up, with citations to several burger chains, about how data produces actions, how strategy emerges from analysis, how the truly defensible advantage was knowing what to do next.

The sorcerer cut him off. He pointed.

Across the road, where there had not been a pond before, there was a pond. A small sign beside it read:

KING BURGER’S ROYAL AMPHIBIAN POND
NOW WITH FLIES

“That was fast.”

“They watched where you built. Someone is always watching where you build.”

“Our research was proprietary.”

“Your research was. Your location wasn’t.”

Some data is private until you use it. Then it becomes a footprint. You spend years learning which customers matter, which workflows are valuable, which market segments are ready, which integrations unlock distribution, which pricing model works, which vertical is secretly desperate, which pond should be built near which road. Then you act. You ship the feature. You enter the vertical. And now everyone else gets to ask a much cheaper question: why did they do that?

The wizard hated this question.

Two frogs left the wizard’s pond and crossed the road. They did not announce themselves. Frogs are not dramatic creatures. They leave in small, wet increments. Six frogs now.

V. Notebook

Throughout this conversation the pond had become lighter. Not dramatically. Wizards notice dramatic things, and ponds, in general, are too dignified to make a scene. But the water level was perhaps an inch below the lip of the largest stone, and the largest stone had been the wizard’s reference point for years.

The sorcerer turned to the apprentice. “Do you understand the pond?”

“Yes.”

“The frogs?”

“Yes.”

“The outcomes?”

“The parts that matter.”

“The parts in the notebook?”

“Some.”

“The parts not in the notebook?”

The apprentice looked at the wizard. Then at the pond, which was now visibly less of a pond than it had been at breakfast.

“Yes.”

The sorcerer nodded. “I’m hiring.”

The wizard stood. “You can’t hire my apprentice.”

“Why not?”

“She knows proprietary things.”

The sorcerer considered this. Then he looked at the apprentice. “Are you proprietary?”

“No,” she said.

She said it gently. The wizard, who had spent a career being told things confidently by people who turned out to be wrong, had no defense against being told something gently by a person who turned out to be right.

“I assumed,” said the wizard.

The sorcerer waited.

“I assumed,” said the wizard again, “that what mattered about the pond was the pond.”

The sorcerer nodded once, slowly.

The apprentice picked up her parchment. She did not pick up the notebook, which was not hers and had never really been about her, although it had quietly become about her in places the wizard had not been measuring.

She left.

The pond was now noticeably lower. The wizard had not seen anyone take any water.

VI. Pond

The pond remained. The frogs remained, the ones still there anyway. The bucket remained, still strategic. The notebook remained under the wizard’s arm, still leather-bound, still labeled.

The wizard opened to a fresh page. At the top, he had written:

UNIQUE PROPRIETARY POND INTELLIGENCE

He stared at it for a long time.

Then he crossed out UNIQUE.

Then PROPRIETARY.

Then INTELLIGENCE.

This left:

POND

Which was accurate, but not especially fundable.

Across the road, King Burger’s pond had a line. The wizard watched another of his frogs climb out of the water and cross over.

From somewhere a small voice said:

“Between six and twelve.”

The wizard looked at the pond.

There were five frogs.

For now.

VII. Parchment

The wizard did what any rational pond-manager does when faced with a shrinking moat and a sudden absence of human overhead: he bought a goblin.

It was a very nice goblin. He leased it for a fraction of the cost of an apprentice’s health insurance. He stood it by the edge of the water, dusted off his hands, and prepared for efficiency.

“Optimize the frogs,” said the wizard.

The goblin blinked. “Please define ‘optimize’ in the context of amphibious asset management.”

The wizard opened his mouth. Then he closed it. He looked at his notebook. He had ten years of data on how many frogs there were, but he suddenly realized, with a very cold and very specific kind of horror, that he had never actually decided what a good number of frogs was. He knew how to measure the pond. He did not know how to run it.

He turned to ask the apprentice, but of course, the apprentice was currently halfway down the road to the sorcerer’s camp.

“Wait,” the wizard yelled after her. “He doesn’t need you! He has the black box! The box can do your job!”

The apprentice stopped. She looked at the sorcerer. It was a fair question. The box had already proved it could count, predict, and reason.

“Why are you hiring me?” she asked.

The sorcerer tapped the black box. “It knows the physics of water. The biology of frogs. The statistical likelihood of dragonflies.”

He paused, the way he paused.

“It does not know what we are trying to do with the pond. Goblins produce text. They do not produce judgment. I have a great many answers. I have very few people who know which questions are worth the asking.”

The apprentice nodded. This made sense. The frontier always gets bigger, but someone still has to decide which part of it to settle.

Across the road, the wizard was arguing with his new goblin about whether a bucket was a feature or a bug.

The apprentice found a comfortable spot on the grass, a safe distance from all of it, and smoothed out her loose piece of parchment. She still had a few things to write down before she officially started the new job.

The sorcerer glanced over her shoulder. “What is that?”

“Nothing.”

“Is it about the pond?”

“A little.”
